content.stem: Liquid penetrant testing detects discontinuities that are:
options: Open to the surface of the part
Fully below the surface with no opening
Only inside magnetic materials
Only in welds
content.explanation: Penetrant must be able to enter the discontinuity, so PT finds only flaws that break through to the surface. A flaw with no surface opening cannot draw in penetrant.
distractors: A flaw with no opening to the surface cannot draw in penetrant and will not show.
PT does not depend on magnetism and works on nonmagnetic materials.
PT is used on welds, castings, forgings, and machined parts alike, not only welds.

content.stem: The physical action that draws penetrant into a fine surface opening is:
options: Capillary action
Magnetic attraction
Electrical current
Gravity alone
content.explanation: Capillary action pulls the liquid into narrow openings, the same effect that draws liquid up a thin tube. It is the core mechanism that makes PT work.
distractors: PT does not rely on magnetism; capillary action draws the penetrant in.
No electrical current is involved in the penetrant process.
Gravity does not pull penetrant into an upward-facing fine crack; capillary action does.

content.stem: PT is suitable for materials that are:
options: Nonporous
Highly porous
Always magnetic
Always nonmetallic
content.explanation: A nonporous surface lets penetrant stay on the surface and in real flaws. A porous material soaks up penetrant everywhere and masks indications.
distractors: A porous material absorbs penetrant across the whole surface and hides indications.
PT works on magnetic and nonmagnetic materials; magnetism is not required.
PT works on many metals as well as some nonmetals; it is not limited to nonmetals.

content.stem: Which discontinuity could PT NOT detect?
options: A subsurface void with sound metal over it
An open surface-breaking crack in it
Surface-connected open porosity pits
A forging lap that is open right to the surface
content.explanation: PT needs a surface opening. A void buried under sound metal has no path for penetrant, so it cannot be found by PT.
distractors: A surface crack is open to the surface and is a typical PT find.
Porosity connected to the surface can draw in penetrant and show.
A lap open to the surface is detectable by PT.

content.stem: PT is classified as which kind of NDT method?
options: A surface method
A volumetric method
A magnetic method
A radiation method
content.explanation: PT reveals flaws open to the surface, so it is a surface examination method, alongside magnetic particle testing.
distractors: Volumetric methods such as radiography and ultrasonics examine through the thickness.
PT does not use magnetism, unlike magnetic particle testing.
PT uses liquids, not radiation.

content.stem: A common reason to choose PT over magnetic particle testing is that the part is:
options: Nonmagnetic, such as aluminum or austenitic stainless
Always a strongly ferromagnetic plain carbon steel only
Far too small to even inspect at all
Heavily painted over on its top surface
content.explanation: Magnetic particle testing needs a ferromagnetic material. On nonmagnetic metals like aluminum, titanium, or austenitic stainless, PT is used instead.
distractors: Ferromagnetic parts can use magnetic particle testing; PT is chosen when they cannot.
Part size is not the deciding factor between the two methods.
A painted surface is generally cleaned or stripped before PT, not a reason to select it.

content.stem: After excess penetrant is removed and developer is applied, an indication forms because penetrant:
options: Bleeds back out of the flaw into the developer
Evaporates away from the whole part surface entirely
Turns directly into a gas vapor
Dissolves the dry developer coating
content.explanation: Trapped penetrant seeps back out of the discontinuity and spreads into the developer, forming a visible indication larger than the actual flaw.
distractors: Penetrant trapped in the flaw bleeds out; it does not simply evaporate away to form the indication.
Penetrant does not turn to gas in the process.
The developer draws penetrant out; the penetrant does not dissolve it.

content.stem: An advantage of PT is that it:
options: Is simple, low cost, and works on many materials
Finds only the deep subsurface flaws
Requires electrical power right at the part itself
Works fine on porous surfaces too
content.explanation: PT is inexpensive, portable, and applies to a wide range of nonporous materials, which is why it is one of the most widely used NDT methods.
distractors: PT finds surface-breaking flaws, not subsurface ones.
Basic visible penetrant inspection needs no electrical power at the part.
Porous surfaces are unsuitable for PT.

content.stem: A limitation of PT is that it:
options: Cannot find flaws that are not open to the surface
Works only on strongly magnetic ferrous metal parts alone
Cannot be used on any welds at all
Requires heavy radiation shielding too
content.explanation: Because penetrant must enter the flaw, PT is limited to surface-breaking discontinuities and cannot reveal fully internal defects.
distractors: PT works on nonmagnetic parts; it does not require magnetism.
PT is commonly used on welds.
PT uses no ionizing radiation and needs no shielding.

content.stem: A visible (Type 2) penetrant indication is seen by the contrast between:
options: A red penetrant and a white developer background
Two different fluorescent dye colors
Black and clear penetrant liquids only
Magnetic particles set against the whole part surface
content.explanation: Visible dye penetrant is typically red and is read against a white developer under ordinary white light, the red against white giving the contrast.
distractors: Two fluorescent colors do not describe the visible-dye contrast under white light.
Visible PT uses a red dye on a white developer, not black and clear liquids.
Magnetic particles belong to magnetic particle testing, not PT.

content.stem: Fluorescent (Type 1) penetrant indications are viewed under:
options: Ultraviolet (UV-A) light in a darkened area
Bright white room light only, and nothing else
No light at all of any kind whatsoever
Plain infrared heat light only
content.explanation: Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light, so it is inspected in a darkened booth where the glowing indications stand out.
distractors: Fluorescent indications are read under UV-A in low ambient light, not bright white light.
Some light is required; fluorescent indications need UV-A to glow.
Fluorescent penetrant responds to UV-A, not infrared.

content.stem: A good penetrant must wet the surface well, meaning it:
options: Spreads over the surface and into fine openings
Beads up and simply rolls right off the part surface
Dries up almost instantly on it
Reacts badly with the bare metal
content.explanation: Wetting ability lets the penetrant spread across the surface and creep into tight flaws. Poor wetting leaves the liquid beaded and unable to enter openings.
distractors: A liquid that beads up wets poorly and will not enter fine flaws.
Instant drying would prevent the penetrant from entering the flaw during dwell.
Penetrant should not chemically react with the part.

content.stem: Surface tension and wetting ability matter because together they control how well penetrant:
options: Enters and is held in a fine discontinuity
Evaporates right out of the open metal can fast
Conducts an electric current well
Magnetizes the whole part somehow
content.explanation: These properties govern capillary entry into tight openings and how the penetrant is retained there, which determines sensitivity to fine flaws.
distractors: Evaporation from the container is not what these properties are selected to control.
Penetrant performance is not about electrical conduction.
PT does not magnetize the part.

content.stem: Typical discontinuities found by PT include:
options: Cracks, laps, seams, and surface porosity
Deep internal voids only, nothing else
Subsurface inclusions only, and nothing more
Tiny internal magnetic domains
content.explanation: Surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts, and surface porosity are common PT finds because each is open to the surface.
distractors: Deep internal voids with no surface opening are not detectable by PT.
Inclusions fully below the surface are not found by PT.
Magnetic domains are unrelated to penetrant testing.

content.stem: PT can be used on which group of materials?
options: Metals, many plastics, ceramics, and glass that are nonporous
Only plain ferrous steel metals here
Only strongly magnetic ferrous steel alloys, and really nothing else
Only soft, porous, absorbent materials
content.explanation: Any clean, nonporous solid that the penetrant will not damage can be inspected, including most metals and many nonmetals.
distractors: PT is not limited to ferrous metals.
PT does not require magnetic materials.
Porous materials are unsuitable because they absorb penetrant everywhere.

content.stem: The term 'discontinuity' means:
options: An interruption in the normal structure of a part
A perfectly clean, passing final inspection test result
A particular type of dry developer
A common type of cleaning solvent
content.explanation: A discontinuity is any break in the expected material structure. Whether it is rejectable depends on evaluation against acceptance criteria.
distractors: A discontinuity is a condition in the part, not an inspection outcome.
A developer is a process material, not a discontinuity.
A solvent is a cleaning material, not a discontinuity.

content.stem: In PT, an 'indication' is:
options: The visible mark produced by penetrant bleeding from a discontinuity
The actual physical flaw or discontinuity itself buried within the part
The written code acceptance limit value
The penetrant dwell time timer setting
content.explanation: An indication is what the inspector sees, the penetrant bleed-out. It points to a discontinuity but is generally larger than the actual flaw.
distractors: The flaw is the discontinuity; the indication is its visible mark.
Acceptance limits are criteria, not the visible mark.
The dwell timer controls timing, not the indication.

content.stem: PT is widely used largely because it is:
options: Simple to apply and relatively inexpensive
The only method that finds cracks
Able to size subsurface flaws
Faster than all other methods in every case
content.explanation: Its simplicity, low cost, and broad material coverage make PT one of the most common NDT methods in industry.
distractors: Other methods also detect cracks; PT is not unique in that.
PT does not size subsurface flaws; it finds surface-breaking ones.
PT is not always the fastest method for every situation.

content.stem: For penetrant to enter a flaw, the flaw and surface must first be:
options: Clean and dry
Coated with oil
Painted
Magnetized
content.explanation: Contaminants block the opening and stop penetrant from entering. The surface and any flaw must be clean and dry before penetrant is applied.
distractors: Oil in the flaw blocks penetrant entry and must be removed.
Paint bridges and seals openings, preventing penetrant entry.
Magnetizing is unrelated to the penetrant process.

content.stem: A Level I technician in PT is generally qualified to:
options: Perform the penetrant process and record results under direction
Write up the full written acceptance criteria document all by himself
Approve the written test procedures
Certify other PT inspectors too
content.explanation: A Level I performs the test steps and records what is seen, working to a written procedure under a Level II or III. Setting criteria and approving procedures are higher-level responsibilities.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from codes and higher-level personnel, not the Level I.
Approving procedures is a Level III responsibility.
Certifying inspectors is not a Level I function.

content.stem: Final evaluation of an indication against acceptance criteria is normally the responsibility of:
options: A Level II or III
A Level I only
The part operator
The penetrant supplier
content.explanation: Performing and recording is Level I work; interpreting and evaluating indications against the acceptance standard is generally done at Level II or above.
distractors: Evaluation to acceptance criteria is above the Level I scope.
The part operator does not evaluate NDT indications.
The penetrant supplier provides materials, not evaluations.

content.stem: Basic visible penetrant inspection is well suited to fieldwork because it:
options: Can be done with portable aerosol cans and no power at the part
Needs a fully darkened darkroom booth
Requires a large, fixed processing tank line setup at all times here
Needs high voltage electrical power too
content.explanation: Solvent-removable visible PT in aerosol form is portable and needs no power or water at the part, making it practical for field use.
distractors: Visible PT does not require a darkroom; that is more associated with fluorescent inspection.
A fixed tank line is a stationary setup, not required for portable visible PT.
PT requires no high voltage.

content.stem: All else equal, very rough surfaces can make PT harder because they:
options: Trap penetrant in surface texture and raise background
Cannot ever be properly cleaned at all well enough beforehand
Repel all of the penetrant clean away
Are always fully porous and open too
content.explanation: Rough texture holds penetrant in the surface irregularities, increasing background that can mask real indications and complicate removal.
distractors: Rough surfaces can be cleaned; the issue is held penetrant in the texture.
Rough surfaces still accept penetrant; they hold too much of it.
Roughness is not the same as porosity, though both raise background.

content.stem: Penetrant materials are generally used within a:
options: Specified temperature range stated by the procedure
A range that simply does not matter at all
A below-freezing temperature range only
A range set well above the boiling point of plain water
content.explanation: Temperature affects penetrant behavior, so a working range is specified. Out-of-range temperatures require qualification before use.
distractors: Temperature does affect the process and is controlled.
PT is not limited to below-freezing operation.
Penetrant is not used above the boiling point of water.

content.stem: PT shows where a discontinuity is, but it does not by itself:
options: Tell you whether the part passes or fails
Produce any visible indication at all itself
Require fully clean, dry surfaces
Use any dry developer at all
content.explanation: The method reveals indications; deciding accept or reject requires evaluating those indications against acceptance criteria, a separate step beyond simply seeing them.
distractors: PT does produce indications; that is its purpose.
PT does require clean surfaces.
PT does use a developer in the standard process.

content.stem: In simplest terms, the penetrant process is:
options: Clean, apply penetrant, remove excess, develop and inspect
Magnetize it, dust it with powder, and then fully demagnetize it
Expose film, develop the film, then interpret
Heat it up, then quench it, then temper
content.explanation: The core PT sequence is to clean the surface, apply penetrant and let it dwell, remove the excess, then apply developer and inspect.
distractors: Magnetize and dust describes magnetic particle testing.
Expose and develop film describes radiography.
Heat, quench, and temper are heat-treatment steps, not PT.

content.stem: The rise of penetrant into a tight crack is most like:
options: Liquid rising in a narrow glass tube
Water flowing freely downhill fast
A magnet picking up loose iron filings
Hot steam condensing on cold glass
content.explanation: A tight crack behaves like a fine capillary tube, where liquid is drawn in against gravity by surface forces. That is the same effect used in PT.
distractors: Downhill flow is gravity-driven, not the capillary effect that fills an upward crack.
Magnetic pickup is unrelated to capillary action.
Condensation is a phase change, not capillary entry.

content.stem: Excess surface penetrant must be removed before developing so that:
options: Only penetrant trapped in flaws remains to form indications
The whole part gets magnetized first
The dry developer step can simply be skipped right over entirely
The whole part surface stays wet
content.explanation: If surface penetrant is left, it masks the bleed-out from real flaws. Removing the excess leaves only penetrant held in discontinuities.
distractors: Removing excess penetrant has nothing to do with magnetizing.
Developer is still applied after removal; it is not skipped.
The surface is dried after removal, not kept wet.

content.stem: Higher penetrant sensitivity generally means the system can reveal:
options: Smaller and tighter discontinuities
Only very large, wide-open surface flaws
Only deep subsurface flaws
Tiny internal magnetic field lines
content.explanation: A more sensitive system detects finer, tighter surface flaws. Higher sensitivity usually comes with more background and stricter process control.
distractors: Higher sensitivity targets smaller flaws, not just large ones.
Sensitivity does not let PT see subsurface flaws.
PT does not detect magnetic fields.

content.stem: Compared with PT, magnetic particle testing has the advantage of:
options: Detecting some near-surface (slightly subsurface) flaws in ferromagnetic parts
Working on absolutely any material at all of any kind whatsoever, every single time
Needing no surface cleaning at all first
Finding only the painted-over defects
content.explanation: Magnetic particle testing can reveal some flaws just below the surface in ferromagnetic materials, which PT cannot, but it is limited to magnetic materials.
distractors: Magnetic particle testing works only on ferromagnetic materials, unlike PT.
Magnetic particle testing also requires surface cleaning.
It detects discontinuities, not painted defects specifically.

content.stem: In general, fluorescent penetrant systems are:
options: More sensitive to fine flaws than visible dye systems
Always far less sensitive overall than visible dye systems
Read under bright white light only
Unable to detect any cracks at all
content.explanation: Fluorescent systems generally detect finer discontinuities than visible dye and are read under UV-A, which is why they are common where high sensitivity is needed.
distractors: Fluorescent systems are generally more, not less, sensitive than visible dye.
Fluorescent indications are read under UV-A, not white light.
Fluorescent penetrant readily detects cracks.

content.stem: A surface indication from PT tells the inspector the flaw's location and length but generally not its:
options: Depth into the material
Presence on the surface
Approximate length
General shape
content.explanation: PT reveals where a flaw is and its surface extent, but it does not directly measure how deep the flaw goes into the part.
distractors: PT does reveal that a flaw is present at the surface.
PT does give an approximate surface length of the indication.
PT does show the general shape of the bleed-out.

content.stem: If a crack is filled with oil or dirt before testing, PT will likely:
options: Miss it, because penetrant cannot enter the blocked opening
Find it far more easily than it normally usually would instead
Show it up much brighter than usual
Size it up much more accurately instead
content.explanation: Contaminant in the flaw blocks penetrant entry, so the flaw may not produce an indication. This is why thorough pre-cleaning is essential.
distractors: A blocked flaw is harder, not easier, to find.
A blocked flaw will not produce a brighter indication; it may produce none.
A blocked flaw is not sized more accurately; it may be missed entirely.

content.stem: Which pair are both surface NDT methods?
options: Penetrant testing and magnetic particle testing
Penetrant testing and film radiography
Ultrasonic testing and film radiography
Eddy current testing and full film radiography only
content.explanation: Penetrant and magnetic particle testing are both surface methods. Radiography and ultrasonics are volumetric.
distractors: Radiography is a volumetric method, not a surface method.
Ultrasonics and radiography are both volumetric methods.
Radiography is volumetric; this pair is not both surface methods.

content.stem: Visible penetrant typically uses a dye that is:
options: Red, for contrast against white developer
Fully clear and colorless, totally see-through
Bright green only under the UV
White, much like the dry developer
content.explanation: Visible dye penetrant is usually red so it stands out against the white developer under ordinary light.
distractors: A colorless penetrant would give no visible contrast.
Glowing only under UV describes fluorescent penetrant, not visible dye.
A white penetrant would blend into the white developer.

content.stem: The developer helps the inspection by:
options: Drawing penetrant out and providing a contrasting background
Cleaning off the whole entire part surface area well beforehand
Magnetizing the whole part first
Sealing up the open surface flaw
content.explanation: Developer pulls trapped penetrant out of flaws and spreads it for visibility, while also providing a background that improves contrast.
distractors: Cleaning is a separate pre-test step, not the developer's job.
Developer does not magnetize the part.
Developer reveals the flaw; it does not seal it.

content.stem: A penetrant indication is usually:
options: Larger than the actual discontinuity, because penetrant spreads in the developer
Exactly the very same size as the actual real discontinuity flaw itself, quite oddly
Smaller than the actual flaw itself
Totally unrelated to the flaw at all
content.explanation: As penetrant bleeds out and spreads in the developer, the visible indication is generally wider than the true flaw, which aids detection but must be considered when judging size.
distractors: The indication is generally larger than the flaw, not exactly its size.
The indication is larger, not smaller, than the flaw.
The indication is directly related to and caused by the flaw.

content.stem: Penetrant materials should be handled with attention to:
options: Manufacturer safety data and proper ventilation
No real safety concerns at all here, whatsoever, ever
High voltage electrical hazards only
Heavy radiation shielding needs only
content.explanation: Penetrant chemicals require following safety data sheets, using ventilation, and wearing appropriate protection. They are not radiation or high-voltage hazards.
distractors: Penetrant chemicals do carry handling and ventilation concerns.
High voltage is not the relevant hazard for penetrant chemicals.
PT does not involve ionizing radiation.

content.stem: A Level I performs PT according to:
options: A written procedure
Personal preference
Whatever is fastest
No documentation
content.explanation: The penetrant process follows an approved written procedure that specifies materials, times, and steps, which the Level I carries out and records.
distractors: Personal preference does not govern a qualified inspection.
Speed does not override the written procedure requirements.
PT requires documented procedures and records.

content.stem: Which statement about PT is correct?
options: It finds surface-breaking flaws on nonporous parts using capillary action
It finds only the deep internal voids
It needs only strongly magnetic materials
It actually works the best only on fully porous, open, and absorbent surfaces
content.explanation: PT uses capillary action to reveal flaws open to the surface of clean, nonporous materials. It does not find buried flaws, does not need magnetism, and does not work on porous surfaces.
distractors: PT does not detect deep internal voids with no surface opening.
PT does not require magnetic materials.
Porous surfaces absorb penetrant and are unsuitable.

content.stem: Penetrants are classified into two types:
options: Type 1 fluorescent and Type 2 visible
Type A and Type B
Type 1 magnetic and Type 2 nonmagnetic
Wet and dry
content.explanation: The two penetrant types are Type 1 (fluorescent, read under UV-A) and Type 2 (visible dye, read under white light).
distractors: Penetrant types are numbered 1 and 2, not lettered A and B; letters designate removal methods.
Penetrants are not classified as magnetic or nonmagnetic.
Wet and dry describe magnetic particle media, not penetrant types.

content.stem: A Type 1 penetrant is:
options: Fluorescent, viewed under UV-A
Visible red dye under white light
A developer
A cleaner
content.explanation: Type 1 is fluorescent penetrant, inspected under ultraviolet (UV-A) light in a darkened area.
distractors: Visible red dye under white light is Type 2, not Type 1.
A developer is a separate process material, not a penetrant type.
A cleaner is not a penetrant type.

content.stem: A Type 2 penetrant is:
options: Visible dye, viewed under white light
Fluorescent dye, viewed only under UV-A
Always a water-washable type only
A dry loose powder developer
content.explanation: Type 2 is visible penetrant, usually red dye, read under ordinary white light against a white developer.
distractors: Fluorescent under UV-A describes Type 1.
Visible penetrant comes in more than one removal method, not water-washable only.
A dry developer is a developer form, not a penetrant type.

content.stem: Penetrant removal methods are designated by:
options: Letters A, B, C, and D
Just the numbers 1 and 2
Penetrant dye colors only
Developer form types only
content.explanation: Methods A, B, C, and D describe how excess penetrant is removed. Types 1 and 2 describe how the penetrant is seen.
distractors: Numbers 1 and 2 designate penetrant type, not removal method.
Colors do not designate removal methods.
Developer forms are a separate classification from removal methods.

content.stem: Method A penetrant is:
options: Water-washable
Post-emulsifiable lipophilic
Solvent-removable
Post-emulsifiable hydrophilic
content.explanation: Method A is water-washable: an emulsifier is built into the penetrant so it can be rinsed off directly with water.
distractors: Post-emulsifiable lipophilic is Method B.
Solvent-removable is Method C.
Post-emulsifiable hydrophilic is Method D.

content.stem: Method B penetrant is:
options: Post-emulsifiable, lipophilic
Fully water-washable type only
Solvent-removable type only
A dry loose powder developer
content.explanation: Method B is post-emulsifiable lipophilic: a separate oil-based emulsifier is applied after dwell so the penetrant can then be water-rinsed.
distractors: Water-washable is Method A.
Solvent-removable is Method C.
A dry developer is not a removal method.

content.stem: Method C penetrant is removed using:
options: A solvent remover (solvent-removable)
A plain water rinse spray only
A hydrophilic water-based emulsifier bath
A simple handheld bar magnet
content.explanation: Method C is solvent-removable: excess penetrant is wiped with a clean cloth and lightly with solvent. It is common in portable aerosol kits.
distractors: Plain water spray alone is the water-washable Method A.
A hydrophilic emulsifier is used in Method D.
Magnets are not used to remove penetrant.

content.stem: Method D penetrant is:
options: Post-emulsifiable, hydrophilic
Solvent-removable type, only
Fully water-washable type, only that
A nonaqueous solvent developer
content.explanation: Method D is post-emulsifiable hydrophilic: a water-based emulsifier (often applied as a bath or spray after a pre-rinse) makes the penetrant water-removable.
distractors: Solvent-removable is Method C.
Water-washable is Method A.
A nonaqueous developer is a developer form, not a removal method.

content.stem: A 'Type 1, Method A' system is:
options: Fluorescent, water-washable
Visible, solvent-removable
Fluorescent, post-emulsifiable
Visible, water-washable
content.explanation: Type 1 is fluorescent and Method A is water-washable, so the combination is a fluorescent water-washable penetrant system.
distractors: Visible, solvent-removable would be Type 2, Method C.
Post-emulsifiable would be Method B or D, not A.
Visible would be Type 2, not Type 1.

content.stem: Penetrant sensitivity levels (such as Level 1/2 through Level 4) apply to:
options: Fluorescent penetrants
Visible color dye penetrants
Dry powder developers only
Solvent surface cleaners
content.explanation: Standardized sensitivity levels are defined for fluorescent penetrants. Visible penetrants are not graded on that numbered sensitivity-level scale.
distractors: Visible penetrants are not classified by the numbered sensitivity-level scale.
Developers are classified by form, not by penetrant sensitivity level.
Cleaners are not graded by penetrant sensitivity level.

content.stem: A higher fluorescent sensitivity level is generally chosen to:
options: Detect finer, tighter discontinuities
Speed up the excess penetrant removal step
Reduce the material cost only
Avoid having to use any developer
content.explanation: Higher sensitivity levels reveal smaller flaws, at the cost of more background and tighter process control. Lower levels suit rougher work where high sensitivity is not needed.
distractors: Sensitivity level is about flaw detection, not removal speed.
Higher sensitivity is not selected merely to cut cost.
Developer is still used regardless of sensitivity level.

content.stem: Developers are supplied in several forms, including:
options: Dry powder, water-based, and nonaqueous (solvent) types
Just Type 1 and Type 2 only
Just Method A and Method B only
Fluorescent and visible dye penetrant types only, nothing else
content.explanation: Developer forms include dry powder, water-soluble, water-suspendable, and nonaqueous solvent-based. Types and methods classify penetrants, not developers.
distractors: Type 1 and Type 2 classify penetrants, not developers.
Method A and B are penetrant removal methods, not developer forms.
Fluorescent and visible describe penetrant types, not developer forms.

content.stem: Dry powder developer is typically used with:
options: Fluorescent penetrant systems
Visible color dye systems only
No penetrant used at all
Solvent surface cleaning only
content.explanation: Dry powder developer is commonly paired with fluorescent penetrant, where the thin powder layer gives good fluorescent indication contrast.
distractors: Dry developer is most associated with fluorescent systems, not visible dye, which usually uses a white nonaqueous developer.
A developer is always used with a penetrant in the standard process.
Dry developer is a process step, not a cleaning-only material.

content.stem: Nonaqueous (solvent-based) developer is supplied as:
options: An aerosol or spray that forms a white coating
A dry, loose powder form only
A plain water immersion bath
A type of red penetrant dye liquid itself, somehow
content.explanation: Nonaqueous developer sprays on as a white solvent-borne coating, common with visible dye for a strong white background, and is widely used in portable kits.
distractors: Dry loose powder is a different developer form.
A water bath describes aqueous developer forms, not nonaqueous.
A developer is not a penetrant.

content.stem: A water-suspendable developer is one in which the developer powder is:
options: Suspended in water and applied as a bath or spray
Fully dissolved completely in a solvent liquid instead
Used completely dry, as a powder only
A type of red penetrant dye
content.explanation: Water-suspendable developer carries the powder suspended in water; the part is coated and then dried so the powder remains.
distractors: Suspended, not dissolved in solvent, describes this aqueous form.
It is applied wet in water, not used dry.
It is a developer, not a penetrant.

content.stem: Penetrant, emulsifier, and developer should be:
options: A compatible family per the procedure, not mixed arbitrarily across brands
Always from completely different brands each
Freely interchangeable with just about any random cleaner at all available out there
Selected only by their outward color
content.explanation: Materials are qualified together as a family. Mixing incompatible products can degrade performance, so the procedure specifies a compatible set.
distractors: Materials are kept within a compatible qualified family, not deliberately mixed across brands.
Cleaners are not freely interchangeable with the penetrant family.
Selection is by qualified family and procedure, not color alone.

content.stem: Post-emulsifiable penetrants (Methods B and D) are used partly because they:
options: Resist over-washing and can give higher sensitivity on fine flaws
Skip the dry developer step entirely
Need no surface cleaning at all
Work only on strongly magnetic ferrous metal parts alone, here always
content.explanation: Because the penetrant is not water-washable until an emulsifier is applied, post-emulsifiable systems resist over-removal and can hold penetrant in fine flaws for higher sensitivity.
distractors: Developer is still used in post-emulsifiable processes.
Pre-cleaning is still required.
These methods are unrelated to magnets.

content.stem: Solvent-removable (Method C) systems are popular for field work because they:
options: Come in portable aerosol cans and need no water line
Require a large, fixed water wash station setup line here
Only work inside a fully dark darkroom
Need electrical power right at the part
content.explanation: Method C aerosol kits are portable and need no water or power at the part, making them practical for field inspection.
distractors: Method C does not require a wash station; that suits water-washable systems.
Visible Method C is read under white light, not only in a darkroom.
Method C needs no electrical power at the part.

content.stem: An emulsifier in post-emulsifiable systems works by:
options: Making the oily penetrant removable with water
Cleaning out the deep subsurface flaws within the part
Developing out the final indication
Magnetizing the whole part surface
content.explanation: The emulsifier combines with the surface penetrant so it can then be rinsed with water. Dwell time of the emulsifier is controlled to avoid over-removal.
distractors: Emulsifiers do not clean subsurface flaws; PT addresses surface-breaking flaws.
The developer, not the emulsifier, forms the indication.
Emulsifiers do not magnetize the surface.

content.stem: The difference between lipophilic (B) and hydrophilic (D) emulsification is that:
options: Lipophilic is oil-based and hydrophilic is water-based
Both of them are fully solvent-based
Lipophilic uses no emulsifier of any kind at all here, ever
Hydrophilic is really just a developer
content.explanation: Lipophilic emulsifier (Method B) is oil-based and diffuses into the penetrant; hydrophilic emulsifier (Method D) is water-based and acts by detergent action, usually after a pre-rinse.
distractors: They differ in base; they are not both solvent-based.
Method B does use an emulsifier; that is what makes it post-emulsifiable.
Hydrophilic emulsifier is a removal aid, not a developer.

content.stem: Penetrant materials should be used:
options: Within their shelf life and not contaminated
After any expiration date has passed
Only when fully separated out into distinct layers
Regardless of their overall condition
content.explanation: Expired or contaminated materials can lose sensitivity. Materials are kept within shelf life and protected from contamination per the procedure.
distractors: Materials past their expiration date should not be used.
Penetrant should be uniform, not separated; separation can indicate a problem.
Condition matters; degraded materials are not used.

content.stem: Visible penetrant relies on color contrast, while fluorescent penetrant relies on:
options: Brightness contrast under UV-A in low ambient light
Magnetic field line contrast only
Color dye contrast seen under bright white room light only
Radiographic film density contrast
content.explanation: Fluorescent indications glow brightly under UV-A against a dark background, a brightness contrast, while visible dye depends on red-against-white color contrast.
distractors: Magnetic contrast is not how penetrant indications are seen.
Color contrast under white light describes visible, not fluorescent, penetrant.
Radiographic density is unrelated to penetrant viewing.

content.stem: Choosing among removal methods depends mainly on:
options: Required sensitivity, surface roughness, and available facilities
The inspector's own current personal mood on that day, somehow, oddly
The outer color of the whole part
The current time of the day it is
content.explanation: Method selection weighs the sensitivity needed, surface condition, part geometry, and whether water, solvent, and booths are available.
distractors: Method selection is technical, not based on mood.
Part color does not drive method selection.
Time of day does not determine the removal method.

content.stem: Penetrant type (1 or 2) and removal method (A through D) are:
options: Independent classifications that combine
Exactly the very same thing really
Both only about the dry developers
Both only about the viewing lighting setup
content.explanation: Type describes how the penetrant is seen and method describes how excess is removed; the two combine, for example Type 1 Method D.
distractors: They are separate classifications, not the same.
Neither classifies developers.
Neither classifies lighting directly.

content.stem: Water-washable (Method A) penetrant is convenient but can be prone to:
options: Over-washing, which removes penetrant from shallow flaws
Never washing off at all ever
Needing a whole extra separate emulsifier step too, somehow here
Only working under the UV-A light
content.explanation: Because the emulsifier is built in, water-washable penetrant can be over-rinsed, stripping penetrant from shallow or broad flaws if wash is not controlled.
distractors: Water-washable penetrant rinses off readily; the risk is over-washing.
Method A needs no separate emulsifier; it is built in.
Method A is available in both visible and fluorescent and is not UV-only.

content.stem: Across all forms, the purpose of a developer is to:
options: Draw out penetrant and provide a contrasting background
Remove all of the excess surface penetrant right off beforehand
Apply the red penetrant dye onto it
Clean off the whole part first
content.explanation: Every developer form serves to blot penetrant from flaws and present it for viewing against a contrasting background, regardless of whether it is dry or wet.
distractors: Removing excess penetrant is the removal step, not the developer's role.
The developer does not apply the penetrant.
Cleaning is a separate pre-test step.

content.stem: Compared with nonaqueous developer, aqueous (water-based) developers generally:
options: Cover large or many parts efficiently but may give slightly lower contrast
Are always far more sensitive overall than any other type of developer out there
Need no drying step at all here
Are used only in spray aerosol cans
content.explanation: Aqueous developers suit batch processing of many or large parts; nonaqueous spray often gives the strongest contrast for critical local areas.
distractors: Aqueous developers are not categorically more sensitive than nonaqueous.
Aqueous developers require a drying step.
Aqueous developers are applied by immersion or spray baths, not only aerosols.

content.stem: Penetrant should appear, as supplied:
options: Uniform, without separation or heavy sediment
Separated out into several distinct visible layers
Cloudy with heavy bottom sediment
Fully dried out and hardened
content.explanation: A good penetrant is a uniform liquid. Separation, heavy sediment, or drying out can signal degradation and a need to replace it.
distractors: Separation into layers can indicate a problem with the material.
Heavy sediment suggests contamination or degradation.
Dried-out penetrant is unusable.

content.stem: Knowing the type and method designation of a system tells the technician:
options: How to view indications and how to remove excess penetrant
The whole part's full heat treatment and its history, somehow
The full welding procedure used
The radiographic film exposure technique
content.explanation: The type tells you the lighting and viewing (UV-A or white light) and the method tells you the removal step, both of which the technician must perform correctly.
distractors: Heat treatment is unrelated to penetrant classification.
Weld procedures are separate from penetrant designation.
Radiographic technique is a different method entirely.

content.stem: Topping off a fluorescent penetrant tank with a different brand or type is:
options: Not allowed unless qualified, since it can alter performance
Just plain standard daily practice everywhere, always, as a rule
Required to be done every single day
A good way to raise the sensitivity
content.explanation: Mixing products can change sensitivity and washability unpredictably, so materials are kept to the qualified family and replenished with the same product.
distractors: Mixing brands or types is not standard and is generally prohibited without qualification.
Daily mixing of different products is not required or appropriate.
Mixing does not reliably raise sensitivity and can degrade it.

content.stem: Because Type 1 penetrant is read under UV-A, inspection is done:
options: In a darkened area with low ambient white light
In bright, direct outdoor sunlight
Without any UV-A black light source present at all
With the red penetrant totally absent
content.explanation: Fluorescent indications are best seen when ambient white light is low and the UV-A source illuminates the part, so a darkened booth or area is used.
distractors: Bright sunlight washes out fluorescent indications.
A UV-A source is required to make fluorescent penetrant glow.
The penetrant must be present in flaws to form indications.

content.stem: Type 2 visible penetrant is read under:
options: Adequate white light
UV-A black light alone
No light at all here
Plain infrared heat light
content.explanation: Visible dye indications are viewed under sufficient white light, where the red dye contrasts with the white developer.
distractors: UV-A is for fluorescent (Type 1) penetrant.
Visible inspection requires adequate white light.
Infrared is not used for penetrant viewing.

content.stem: Which system is most often supplied as a three-can aerosol kit (cleaner, penetrant, developer)?
options: Type 2, Method C (visible, solvent-removable)
Type 1, Method A system only
Type 1, Method D system only
Just about any fluorescent dye system at all really
content.explanation: Visible solvent-removable kits (Type 2, Method C) are the familiar three-aerosol field sets: cleaner/remover, penetrant, and nonaqueous developer.
distractors: Type 1 Method A is a fluorescent water-wash line, typically a tank process.
Type 1 Method D is a fluorescent post-emulsifiable tank process.
Fluorescent systems generally need UV-A and are not the typical white-light aerosol field kit.

content.stem: Selecting a very high fluorescent sensitivity level on a rough surface can:
options: Raise background that makes real indications harder to judge
Always improve the final overall results greatly, somehow, oddly
Remove the need for any surface cleaning
Eliminate the dry developer step
content.explanation: On rough or broad surfaces, very high sensitivity can produce excessive background and irrelevant indications, so the level is matched to the work.
distractors: Higher sensitivity is not always better; it can hurt readability on rough work.
Cleaning is still required regardless of sensitivity level.
Developer is still used regardless of sensitivity level.

content.stem: The specific type, method, and sensitivity for a job are set by:
options: The governing specification and written procedure
The technician chosen at total random
The part's outer surface color
The ambient room air temperature alone, oddly enough
content.explanation: The applicable specification and procedure define which materials and classifications to use; the technician follows them rather than choosing arbitrarily.
distractors: Material selection is not random; it follows the specification.
Part color does not set the classification.
Temperature is controlled but does not by itself set the classification.

content.stem: Which pairing is correct?
options: Type 1 fluorescent / Type 2 visible; Methods A, B, C, D for removal
Type A and B penetrant types only
Methods 1 and 2 used for the viewing
The dry developers are themselves Type 1 and Type 2 only, here as a rule
content.explanation: Penetrant type is 1 (fluorescent) or 2 (visible); removal methods are A (water-washable), B (lipophilic post-emulsifiable), C (solvent-removable), and D (hydrophilic post-emulsifiable).
distractors: Penetrants are Types 1 and 2, not Types A and B.
Viewing relates to type (1 or 2), not methods numbered 1 and 2.
Developers are classified by form, not as Type 1 and Type 2.

content.stem: Pre-cleaning before penetrant application is important because:
options: Contaminants block flaws and prevent penetrant from entering
It magnetizes the whole part somehow
It actually speeds up the drying of the dry developer coating later
It replaces the dry developer entirely
content.explanation: Oil, dirt, paint, and other contaminants seal off flaw openings. If penetrant cannot enter, the flaw will not show, so the surface and flaws must be clean.
distractors: Cleaning does not magnetize the part.
Cleaning prepares the surface; it is not about developer drying.
Cleaning is a separate step and does not replace the developer.

content.stem: Common contaminants that must be removed before PT include:
options: Oil, grease, dirt, paint, rust, and scale
Only surface fingerprints, and nothing else
Only plain water droplets, nothing more
Nothing at all needs any removal
content.explanation: Any material that blocks the opening or holds penetrant on the surface must be removed: oils, greases, dirt, paint, coatings, rust, and scale.
distractors: Fingerprints are only one of many contaminants to address.
Water is one concern, but oils, paint, and scale also matter.
Surfaces must be cleaned; contaminants do affect results.

content.stem: Solvent cleaning removes contaminants by:
options: Dissolving oils and greases so they can be wiped away
Magnetizing the whole part surface completely somehow first
Adding more red penetrant dye
Coating the whole part surface white
content.explanation: Solvent dissolves oils and greases; wiping with clean cloths then removes the loosened contaminant. Final wipes use clean material to avoid redepositing.
distractors: Solvent cleaning does not magnetize the part.
Cleaning removes contaminants; it does not add penetrant.
Coating white is a developer function, not cleaning.

content.stem: Aggressive mechanical methods like shot blasting or wire brushing can be a problem before PT because they:
options: Can smear metal over and close flaw openings
Always clean out all the flaws perfectly well somehow
Add more penetrant right into the flaw
Improve the overall sensitivity greatly
content.explanation: Blasting, grinding, or brushing can peen or smear metal across openings, sealing flaws so penetrant cannot enter. Etching may be needed to reopen worked surfaces.
distractors: These methods can close flaws rather than clean them out.
Mechanical cleaning does not add penetrant.
Smearing metal over flaws lowers, not improves, sensitivity.

content.stem: Etching is sometimes used before PT to:
options: Remove smeared metal and reopen flaws closed by machining or grinding
Add a colored red penetrant dye onto the whole part surface area somehow
Dry off the whole part surface
Apply the dry developer coat over it
content.explanation: A controlled etch removes a thin smeared layer left by machining or grinding, reopening flaws that were closed so penetrant can enter.
distractors: Etching is a cleaning/conditioning step, not a dye application.
Etching is a wet chemical step; drying follows separately.
Etching does not apply developer.

content.stem: After wet cleaning, the part must be:
options: Dried so trapped cleaner or water does not block penetrant
Left fully soaking wet on purpose for the penetrant step somehow
Immediately painted over on top
Fully magnetized beforehand first
content.explanation: Residual water or cleaner in a flaw blocks penetrant entry, so the part is dried (allowing time or using warm air) before penetrant is applied.
distractors: A wet flaw will not accept penetrant; drying is required.
Painting would seal flaws; it is not done before PT.
Drying is required, not magnetizing.

content.stem: Paint or coatings on the surface must be:
options: Removed, since they bridge and seal flaw openings
Left fully in place there to protect the flaw itself
Penetrated straight through them
Developed right over the top of them
content.explanation: A coating bridges over openings so penetrant cannot reach the flaw. Coatings are stripped before PT unless a procedure specifically qualifies otherwise.
distractors: Coatings seal flaws and must be removed, not left on.
Penetrant cannot reliably reach a flaw through paint.
Developing over paint does not reveal flaws sealed beneath it.

content.stem: Vapor degreasing cleans parts by:
options: Condensing solvent vapor on the part to dissolve oils
Blasting it really hard with rough abrasive grit somehow
Soaking it deep in penetrant dye
Heating it up to full red heat
content.explanation: In vapor degreasing, hot solvent vapor condenses on the cooler part and dissolves oils and greases, draining away clean. It is effective for oily contamination.
distractors: Grit blasting is mechanical, not vapor degreasing, and can close flaws.
Vapor degreasing uses solvent vapor, not penetrant.
Parts are not heated to red heat for cleaning.

content.stem: Alkaline or detergent cleaners are used to:
options: Remove contaminants in a wash, followed by rinsing and drying
Apply the red penetrant dye onto the whole part surface area first
Develop out the final indications
Magnetize the whole part surface
content.explanation: Alkaline and detergent cleaners lift soils in a wash process; the part is then rinsed and dried before penetrant. These are common for batch cleaning.
distractors: These cleaners prepare the surface; they do not apply penetrant.
They do not develop indications.
They do not magnetize the surface.

content.stem: Ultrasonic cleaning improves cleaning by:
options: Using high-frequency agitation in a cleaning bath to dislodge contaminants
Magnetizing the whole cleaning bath
Adding dry developer into the cleaning bath
Heating the whole part right up to its full melting point somehow, quite oddly
content.explanation: Ultrasonic energy agitates the cleaning solution, helping remove contaminants from intricate surfaces and openings. The part is then rinsed and dried.
distractors: Ultrasonic cleaning does not magnetize anything.
Developer is not part of a cleaning bath.
Parts are not melted during cleaning.

content.stem: The cleaned area should extend:
options: At least over the inspection area plus a surrounding margin
Only a small local spot of it
Nowhere near the actual flaw at all
Out over the whole entire building, somehow, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Cleaning covers the area to be inspected plus a margin around it, so contaminants outside the exact spot do not interfere with processing or viewing.
distractors: A small spot may leave nearby contaminants that interfere.
The flaw area in particular must be clean.
Cleaning the building is not the requirement; the inspection area and margin are.

content.stem: Cleaning agents themselves must be:
options: Removed or evaporated so they leave no interfering residue
Left sitting deep in the flaw
Mixed right into the red penetrant dye itself, somehow quite oddly
Applied on as the dry developer
content.explanation: A cleaner left in a flaw can dilute or block penetrant. Cleaners are chosen and used so they fully evaporate or are rinsed away before penetrant.
distractors: Cleaner left in the flaw interferes with penetrant entry.
Cleaner is not mixed into the penetrant.
Cleaner is not used as developer.

content.stem: After cleaning, the surface should be:
options: Kept free of new contamination such as bare-hand oils
Handled freely with bare, oily hands
Coated all over in heavy grease
Left exposed openly to dust and dirt indefinitely, somehow
content.explanation: Re-contamination undoes the cleaning. Clean parts are protected from oils, dust, and handling until penetrant is applied.
distractors: Bare-hand handling can deposit skin oils and recontaminate the surface.
Grease would recontaminate the cleaned surface.
Leaving the surface to collect dust defeats the cleaning.

content.stem: Drying is critical specifically because liquid left inside a flaw will:
options: Prevent penetrant from filling the flaw
Help the red penetrant dye enter much faster
Improve the overall contrast greatly
Develop out the final indication
content.explanation: A flaw already full of water or solvent has no room for penetrant, so it cannot fill and the flaw may be missed. Adequate drying time is required.
distractors: Liquid in the flaw blocks rather than speeds penetrant entry.
Trapped liquid hurts, not helps, the result.
Trapped liquid does not develop an indication.

content.stem: When warm air or an oven is used to dry parts before penetrant, the temperature must:
options: Stay within procedure limits to avoid harming the part or process
Be made as high as is possible
Always far exceed the red penetrant's own flash point somehow, oddly
Not really matter at all here
content.explanation: Excessive temperature can damage the part or push it outside the penetrant's working range. Drying temperature is kept within the procedure limits.
distractors: Maximum heat is not the goal; controlled drying within limits is.
Drying must not create a fire hazard near flammable penetrant.
Temperature does matter for both the part and the process.

content.stem: If a machined surface still hides flaws after normal cleaning, the likely issue is:
options: Smeared metal closing the openings, which may require etching
Far too much red penetrant dye being used on it somehow, quite oddly
Far too much dry developer used
Far too much excess UV-A light
content.explanation: Machining can smear a thin metal layer over flaws. Standard cleaning will not reopen them, so etching is used to remove the smeared layer.
distractors: Excess penetrant is a removal issue, not the cause of closed openings.
Excess developer does not close machined-over flaws.
UV light intensity is unrelated to closed openings.

content.stem: Abrasive blasting before PT, when permitted, is a concern mainly on:
options: Soft metals where openings can be peened closed
Very hard ceramic parts only
Already fully painted-over parts
Strongly magnetic ferrous metal parts only, here always
content.explanation: Soft or ductile metals are especially prone to having flaw openings peened shut by blasting media, so blasting is used cautiously and may be followed by etching.
distractors: The peening-closed concern is greatest on soft metals, not just ceramics.
Paint is removed before PT; the concern here is closing flaws.
The concern applies to nonmagnetic soft metals too, not only magnetic parts.

content.stem: Before applying a hydrophilic emulsifier (Method D), a pre-rinse is often used to:
options: Remove the bulk of surface penetrant first
Add even more red penetrant dye right onto it
Dry out the open flaw first
Develop out the whole part early
content.explanation: A water pre-rinse knocks down most of the surface penetrant so the hydrophilic emulsifier works more evenly and controllably on what remains.
distractors: A pre-rinse removes surface penetrant; it does not add penetrant.
A pre-rinse uses water and does not dry the flaw.
Developing is a later step, not the pre-rinse.

content.stem: Whether cleaning was adequate can be judged by:
options: A clean, contaminant-free surface and acceptable background in results
The whole part's overall weight
The outer printed color of the dry developer spray can itself, quite oddly
The current time of the day it is now
content.explanation: A properly cleaned surface looks free of soils, and excessive background or false indications in the result can signal incomplete cleaning.
distractors: Part weight does not indicate cleaning quality.
Developer can color is unrelated to cleaning verification.
Time of day does not verify cleaning.

content.stem: Cleaners used before PT should be:
options: Compatible with the part and the penetrant family
Just any random chemical at all, literally anything
Always just the dry developer
Always just plain water only
content.explanation: Cleaners are chosen so they do not damage the part or leave residues incompatible with the penetrant. The procedure specifies acceptable cleaners.
distractors: Random chemicals may damage the part or interfere with penetrant.
The developer is not a cleaner.
Water alone is not always sufficient for oils and greases.

content.stem: Before applying penetrant, the part temperature should be:
options: Within the procedure's allowed range
As very hot as is possible
Below the freezing point of water always
Totally irrelevant here somehow
content.explanation: Penetrant behavior depends on temperature, so the part is brought within the specified range before application; out-of-range work requires qualification.
distractors: Excessive heat can dry penetrant before it enters flaws.
Below freezing is not a general requirement and can be out of range.
Part temperature does matter for the process.

content.stem: Loose rust and scale must be removed because they:
options: Hold penetrant on the surface and can cover flaws
Improve the natural capillary action greatly somehow
Are required for the developing step
Magnetize the whole part surface
content.explanation: Rust and scale create false background and can cover openings, so they are removed by appropriate cleaning before penetrant is applied.
distractors: Rust and scale hinder, not improve, the process.
They are contaminants, not a developing aid.
They are not used to magnetize the surface.

content.stem: In the overall process, pre-cleaning comes:
options: First, before penetrant is applied
After the developing step only
After the final inspection only
In between removal and the developing
content.explanation: Cleaning is the first step so penetrant can enter the flaws. It precedes penetrant application, removal, developing, and inspection.
distractors: Cleaning precedes, not follows, developing.
Cleaning is done before, not after, inspection.
Cleaning is the first step, not a step inserted before developing.

content.stem: When solvent-wiping a surface clean, the technician should:
options: Use clean cloths and avoid redepositing contaminant
Reuse the very dirtiest old rag
Pour solvent right down into the open flaws and leave it there
Skip doing the final clean wipe step
content.explanation: Final wipes use clean material so contaminant is removed rather than smeared back. Solvent is not flooded into flaws and left to block them.
distractors: A dirty rag redeposits contaminant on the surface.
Solvent left in flaws blocks penetrant entry.
A clean final wipe is needed to finish the job properly.

content.stem: Cleaning a margin around the inspection area helps prevent:
options: Contaminant from edges migrating into the test area
The whole part from drying out
The red penetrant from entering any of the open flaws at all
The dry developer from working at all
content.explanation: A clean surrounding margin keeps nearby contaminant from creeping into the inspection zone during processing.
distractors: A margin does not stop the part from drying.
Cleaning helps, not hinders, penetrant entry.
Cleaning does not stop the developer from working.

content.stem: An acceptable way to dry a part after aqueous cleaning is:
options: Allowing dwell in warm air within temperature limits
Wiping it all down with a dirty, oily old rag somehow first
Dipping it deep in penetrant dye
Coating it all over with grease
content.explanation: Warm-air drying within limits, or adequate ambient drying time, removes water before penetrant. Oil or grease would recontaminate the surface.
distractors: An oily rag recontaminates the surface.
Penetrant is not used to dry the part.
Grease would recontaminate, not dry, the part.

content.stem: A thin coating may be left on a part for PT only when:
options: A qualified procedure specifically permits it
The technician just decides to save some time, somehow
It is always fully acceptable anyway
The coating happens to be colorful
content.explanation: Coatings normally must be removed, but a specific qualified procedure may allow inspection through a thin coating in defined cases. Absent that, coatings are stripped.
distractors: Skipping coating removal to save time is not acceptable.
Leaving coatings is not always acceptable; it is the exception.
Coating color is irrelevant to whether it may remain.

content.stem: After etching, the part must be:
options: Neutralized/rinsed and dried before penetrant
Coated all over in heavy oil
Left soaking wet with the strong acid etchant still
Developed right away immediately after
content.explanation: Etchant residue must be removed and the part dried, or it will interfere with penetrant. Etching is followed by rinsing, neutralizing as required, and drying.
distractors: Oil would recontaminate the surface.
Etchant left on the surface interferes with penetrant.
Developing does not follow directly after etching; cleaning and drying do.

content.stem: Skin oils from bare-hand handling matter because they:
options: Can recontaminate a cleaned surface and cause background
Improve the red penetrant's entry
Develop out the final indication
Are actually required by the written test procedure here, oddly
content.explanation: Oils transferred from hands add contamination that can create background or block flaws, so clean parts are handled carefully, often with gloves.
distractors: Skin oils hinder, not help, penetrant entry.
They do not develop indications.
Procedures aim to avoid such contamination, not require it.

content.stem: The single biggest reason careful cleaning matters is that:
options: Penetrant cannot enter a flaw that is blocked by contamination
Cleaning somehow sets the dry developer's final color, quite oddly
It magnetizes the ferrous metal parts
It shortens the dwell time right to zero
content.explanation: If contamination blocks the opening, penetrant cannot enter and the flaw is missed. Cleaning is the foundation of a valid penetrant test.
distractors: Cleaning does not set developer color.
Cleaning does not magnetize parts.
Dwell time is still required after cleaning.

content.stem: The cleaning method used is:
options: Specified by the procedure and part of doing the test correctly
Left entirely up to random chance
Never relevant at all here, ever
Chosen just to match the part's outer surface color somehow, oddly
content.explanation: The procedure specifies acceptable cleaning so results are repeatable and valid. The technician follows it as part of performing the test.
distractors: Cleaning is specified, not left to chance.
Cleaning method is relevant to a valid test.
Part color does not determine the cleaning method.

content.stem: Which statement about surface preparation is correct?
options: The surface and flaws must be clean and dry before penetrant is applied
Wet flaws improve the final results
Paint should just be left on it
Smearing metal over the open flaws actually helps the detection a lot here
content.explanation: A clean, dry surface with open flaws is required. Wet or contaminated flaws, coatings, and smeared metal all prevent penetrant from entering.
distractors: Wet flaws block penetrant and hurt results.
Paint bridges flaws and must be removed.
Smeared metal closes flaws and reduces detection.

content.stem: Penetrant can be applied by:
options: Spraying, brushing, dipping, or flowing it onto the surface
Magnetizing the whole part completely first, somehow, quite oddly enough
Heating the whole part up hot
Developing the whole part first
content.explanation: Penetrant is applied by aerosol spray, brush, immersion (dip), or flow-on, whatever evenly covers the inspection area. The method is chosen to suit the part and process.
distractors: Magnetizing is not how penetrant is applied.
Heating is not a penetrant application method.
Developing comes after penetrant, not before.

content.stem: When applying penetrant, the technician must ensure:
options: The entire inspection area is covered and stays wet during dwell
Only a small local spot of it gets lightly wetted somehow, oddly enough
The whole surface dries up immediately
The dry developer is mixed right in
content.explanation: The whole area of interest must be coated and kept wet with penetrant throughout the dwell so penetrant can enter all flaws.
distractors: Partial coverage can miss flaws in uncovered areas.
The penetrant must stay wet during dwell, not dry immediately.
Developer is not mixed into the penetrant.

content.stem: Dwell time is the period during which:
options: Penetrant is left on the surface to seep into flaws
The dry developer draws the trapped penetrant back out
The whole part is cleaned off
The surface excess is removed
content.explanation: Dwell time lets capillary action draw penetrant into discontinuities. Too little dwell can miss fine flaws.
distractors: Developer drawing penetrant out is development, a later step.
Cleaning happens before penetrant application, not during dwell.
Removal of excess follows the dwell, it is not the dwell itself.

content.stem: If dwell time is too short:
options: Penetrant may not fully enter fine flaws, and they can be missed
The flaws are always still all found anyway somehow, quite oddly enough
The dry developer simply fails
The whole part overheats badly
content.explanation: Insufficient dwell does not give penetrant time to fill tight flaws, so fine discontinuities may produce weak or no indications.
distractors: Short dwell can cause fine flaws to be missed, not always found.
Developer function is separate from dwell time.
Short dwell does not overheat the part.

content.stem: Required dwell time depends on:
options: Material, expected flaw type, penetrant, and temperature
Only the inspector's own personal preference on the given day
The part's outer surface color
The brand of wiping cloth being used
content.explanation: Dwell is set by the procedure based on the material, the kind and tightness of flaws sought, the penetrant used, and the temperature.
distractors: Dwell is specified, not based on preference.
Part color does not set dwell time.
Cloth brand is irrelevant to dwell time.

content.stem: During dwell, the penetrant must NOT be allowed to:
options: Dry on the surface
Enter into the open flaws
Stay fully wet on it
Cover the whole test area
content.explanation: If penetrant dries on the surface, it becomes hard to remove and can leave heavy background. The surface is kept wet, reapplying penetrant if needed during long dwells.
distractors: Penetrant entering flaws is exactly what dwell is for.
Penetrant should stay wet during dwell.
Penetrant should cover the area during dwell.

content.stem: For a long dwell, if the surface starts to dry the technician should:
options: Reapply penetrant to keep the surface wet
Just let it fully dry out and then continue on
Apply the dry developer over it
Wash it all off and just stop
content.explanation: To keep flaws filling and avoid dried-on penetrant, more penetrant is applied to maintain a wet surface through the required dwell.
distractors: Letting it dry causes removal problems and heavy background.
Developer is not applied during the penetrant dwell.
Washing off and stopping abandons the test rather than maintaining dwell.

content.stem: At lower temperatures, penetrant tends to be more viscous, so dwell time may need to be:
options: Longer, or the temperature brought into range
Made much shorter instead
Fully eliminated entirely instead
Replaced by more dry developer time instead, somehow
content.explanation: Cold penetrant flows and enters flaws more slowly. Procedures address this by allowing longer dwell or by bringing the part within the qualified temperature range.
distractors: Cold, viscous penetrant generally needs more, not less, dwell.
Dwell is still required; it cannot be eliminated.
More developer does not compensate for inadequate dwell.

content.stem: Dip (immersion) application is well suited to:
options: Many small parts processed together in a basket
One single huge structure out in the open field somewhere
Parts that cannot ever get wet at all
The final developing step only
content.explanation: Immersion coats many small parts at once efficiently in a tank line. Large field structures are usually sprayed or brushed instead.
distractors: A single huge field structure is not practical to immerse.
Immersion applies liquid penetrant, so parts must tolerate wetting.
Immersion applies penetrant; it is not a developing method.

content.stem: Aerosol spray application is common in:
options: Portable solvent-removable field kits
Large, fixed immersion tank line setups only
Dry developer powder bed setups only
Magnetic yoke testing work only
content.explanation: Aerosol penetrant is convenient for field and spot inspection, typically in the three-can solvent-removable kit.
distractors: Immersion lines use tanks, not aerosols.
Dry powder beds are a developing method, not penetrant application.
Magnetic yoke testing is a different method entirely.

content.stem: Penetrant should be applied as:
options: An even, continuous film over the inspection area
A few scattered loose drops here and there only, somehow
A thick, heavy crust layer
A dry, light powder dusting
content.explanation: A uniform, continuous wet film ensures every part of the area and every flaw is in contact with penetrant during dwell.
distractors: Scattered drops leave gaps where flaws could be missed.
A crust forms from dried penetrant and causes problems.
Penetrant is a liquid film, not a dry dusting.

content.stem: Tilting or hanging immersed parts to let excess drain during dwell helps:
options: Avoid pooling and uneven dwell while flaws fill
Speed up the part's overall magnetization somehow, oddly
Apply the dry developer on
Heat the whole part up fast
content.explanation: Allowing excess to drain during dwell prevents thick pooling and keeps a workable film while flaws fill, supporting consistent results.
distractors: Draining is unrelated to magnetization.
Draining does not apply developer.
Draining does not heat the part.

content.stem: Very tight or fine flaws generally require:
options: More dwell time to fill than wide, open flaws
Much less dwell time overall here, oddly enough
No dwell time at all needed
Only the dry developer step
content.explanation: Tight openings fill more slowly by capillary action, so fine flaws need adequate dwell. Wide flaws fill faster.
distractors: Tight flaws need more, not less, dwell.
Dwell is always required for penetrant to enter.
Developer alone does not substitute for dwell.

content.stem: Procedures often set a maximum dwell as well as a minimum because:
options: Penetrant can dry out and become hard to remove if left too long
A longer dwell time is always far better here, in every single case
The whole part will rust up
The dry developer expires
content.explanation: Beyond a maximum, penetrant dries on the surface, causing removal difficulty and background. So both a minimum and a maximum dwell are specified.
distractors: Longer is not always better; over-dwell causes drying problems.
Dwell limits are about penetrant behavior, not part rusting.
Developer shelf life is a separate matter from dwell limits.

content.stem: Before starting the dwell timer, the technician should confirm:
options: The full area is wetted with penetrant
The dry developer is already on it somehow
The whole part is magnetized first
The viewing booth is fully bright
content.explanation: Dwell timing begins once the area is fully coated. Confirming complete coverage ensures all flaws have the full dwell to fill.
distractors: Developer is applied after removal, not before dwell.
Magnetization is not part of PT.
Booth brightness is a viewing condition, not a coverage check.

content.stem: Uneven penetrant application can lead to:
options: Some flaws not filling, risking missed indications
Far better overall sensitivity, somehow, oddly enough
Much faster developing overall
No real effect at all here
content.explanation: Areas that receive little or no penetrant may not fill their flaws, so uneven application risks missing real discontinuities.
distractors: Uneven application hurts, not helps, sensitivity.
It does not speed development and can cause uneven results.
Uneven application does affect the outcome.

content.stem: Brush application is useful for:
options: Applying penetrant to localized areas or complex spots
Coating many thousands of small parts all at once together
Drying off the whole part
Reading off the final indications
content.explanation: Brushing places penetrant on specific local areas or hard-to-reach features. Bulk processing uses immersion or spray.
distractors: Brushing is slow for very large batches; immersion suits those.
Brushing applies penetrant; it does not dry the part.
Reading indications is the inspection step, not application.

content.stem: Standard penetrant procedures are typically qualified for a moderate temperature range, and use outside that range requires:
options: Qualification of the technique at the new temperature
Nothing special at all needed
Doubling up the whole amount of dry developer used somehow
Skipping the dwell time entirely
content.explanation: Procedures specify a temperature range. Working hotter or colder than that range requires qualifying the process at the new condition, often against a reference comparison.
distractors: Out-of-range temperature does require special handling.
Adding developer does not address temperature qualification.
Dwell cannot be skipped for out-of-range temperature.

content.stem: Dwell time is generally measured from:
options: When penetrant is applied until removal begins
When the dry developer is applied
When the whole part first gets cleaned off properly
When the final inspection ends
content.explanation: Dwell runs from penetrant application to the start of excess removal. It is the time available for penetrant to enter flaws.
distractors: Developer application is after dwell and removal.
Cleaning precedes penetrant application.
Inspection is the final step, after developing.

content.stem: Excess pooled penetrant in cavities should be:
options: Allowed to drain so it does not complicate removal
Left there to fully harden up
Sealed right in there tight
Developed right away immediately, very fast, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Pooled penetrant in recesses is drained during dwell so the later removal step is manageable and background is controlled.
distractors: Hardened penetrant is difficult to remove and causes background.
Sealing pooled penetrant in causes removal problems.
Developing immediately skips required removal.

content.stem: When spraying penetrant, the technician should:
options: Use adequate ventilation and follow safety guidance
Spray inside a sealed, unventilated room
Avoid all protective safety measures entirely, somehow oddly
Spray it directly toward other people
content.explanation: Spraying creates mist, so ventilation and proper protection are used per the safety data. Penetrant is applied responsibly and not toward people.
distractors: A sealed unventilated room concentrates mist and vapor.
Protective measures are part of safe application.
Spraying toward others is unsafe.

content.stem: For consistent results across many parts, dwell time should be:
options: Controlled the same way for each part per the procedure
Made totally different each and every single time, somehow
Fully ignored entirely each time
Set just by the part's overall weight
content.explanation: Applying the same controlled dwell to each part keeps results comparable and valid. The procedure defines the dwell to use.
distractors: Random dwell yields inconsistent results.
Dwell cannot be ignored.
Part weight does not set dwell time.

content.stem: Applying penetrant to a part that is too hot can:
options: Dry the penetrant before it enters flaws
Improve the overall flaw filling quite a lot
Lengthen the usable dwell time
Have no real effect at all
content.explanation: On an overheated part, penetrant evaporates or dries before capillary action fills the flaws, so part temperature is kept within range.
distractors: Overheating hinders, not helps, flaw filling.
Heat shortens, not lengthens, usable dwell.
Excess heat does affect the process.

content.stem: Flow-on application means:
options: Pouring or flowing penetrant over the surface to coat it
Brushing on a thin narrow line
Dusting on dry developer powder all over the whole part somehow
Wiping it down with a solvent
content.explanation: In flow-on application the penetrant is poured or flowed over the part to wet the area, useful for large parts that cannot be immersed.
distractors: Brushing a line is brush application, not flow-on.
Dusting powder is developing, not penetrant application.
Wiping with solvent is cleaning or removal, not penetrant application.

content.stem: The dwell time used is something the Level I technician should:
options: Follow per procedure and be able to record
Choose freely on a whim and then just forget it
Keep it a total secret somehow
Replace with the dry developer time
content.explanation: Dwell is a controlled parameter taken from the procedure; the technician applies it and records the process as required for traceability.
distractors: Dwell is specified, not freely chosen and forgotten.
Process parameters are documented, not secret.
Developer time is a separate parameter from dwell.

content.stem: The correct order is:
options: Apply penetrant, then allow dwell, then remove excess
Remove the surface excess first, then apply the penetrant
Develop it first, then apply the penetrant
Inspect it first, then apply the penetrant
content.explanation: Penetrant is applied, allowed to dwell, and only then is the excess removed, before developing and inspecting.
distractors: Removal comes after, not before, applying penetrant.
Developing follows removal, not precedes penetrant.
Inspection is the last step, not before penetrant.

content.stem: On vertical or overhead surfaces, the technician must ensure penetrant:
options: Stays in contact with the area for the full dwell
Runs right off almost immediately
Is applied just one single time and then fully ignored
Dries up before the dwell even starts
content.explanation: Penetrant can run off vertical and overhead surfaces, so it is reapplied as needed to maintain a wet film for the full dwell.
distractors: Penetrant running off shortens contact and can miss flaws.
It may need reapplication, not a single ignored coat.
Drying before dwell completes defeats the purpose.

content.stem: Within limits, giving adequate dwell helps:
options: Fine flaws fill and produce detectable indications
Reduce the overall sensitivity quite a lot somehow, oddly
Skip the surface cleaning step
Skip the developing step entirely
